problem: Goal-oriented VLN methods focus on navigation and neglect object grounding at the endpoint, leaving a large gap between navigation success and grounding success (e.g. on REVERIE and SOON). Traditional grounding methods struggle with the complex instruction reasoning and multi-view synthesis required.
motivation: Real-world goal-oriented navigation requires identifying the target object at the destination, not just arriving. Instructions demand complex reasoning and combining multi-perspective images, which overwhelms conventional grounding modules; MLLMs are strong at such reasoning.
key_idea: Let the VLN agent ask an MLLM for help when it is unsure about the target object, after a multi-stage evaluation of the cause of confusion and extraction of the most relevant information, in a plug-and-play, retraining-free manner.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation evidence can be cited. The abstract suggests that the bottleneck in goal-oriented VLN is endpoint grounding rather than navigation, and that selectively querying an MLLM with relevant, updated information can close this gap without retraining.
method: Assistance trigger: the agent decides when it is struggling to locate the target object and seeks help from an MLLM.
Multi-stage evaluation: the agent discerns the cause of its confusion (details not given in the abstract).
Information extraction and update: the most relevant information is extracted and updated as input for the MLLM to assess.
MLLM grounding: an MLLM reasons over the instruction and multi-view object images to select the target object.
Plug-and-play integration: model-agnostic, applied to existing VLN methods without retraining.

setting.backbone: MLLM (unspecified in abstract) on top of existing VLN agents
setting.observation: multi-view egocentric RGB images of objects/panoramas (inferred)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (inferred from REVERIE/SOON base agents)

results: The abstract reports that applying the approach to four different VLN methods improves performance on REVERIE and SOON, showing effectiveness and generalizability. No specific numbers are given.
limitations: Depends on an external MLLM, adding inference cost and latency.
